analysis.one_liner: Bans members of Congress from trading individual stocks and taking paid lobbying jobs after leaving office.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced by one senator, referred to a committee, never received a vote, and died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have barred sitting members of Congress from buying or selling individual company stocks (they could still hold broad mutual or index funds), banned former members from ever taking paid lobbying or policy-influencing jobs, required presidential and vice-presidential candidates to make their last ten years of tax returns public, barred the President, Vice President, Cabinet members, and their immediate families from soliciting money from foreign governments and foreign-controlled entities, and extended the existing ban on foreign money to state and local ballot initiative campaigns. It was referred to the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens, who would gain a clearer view of whether lawmakers' financial interests overlap with their official duties. The bill would also have protected voters from foreign money in state ballot fights, and the public interest in knowing candidates for the presidency are not financially entangled abroad.

how_it_helps.text: It bans members of Congress from buying or selling individual stocks, with violations punishable by up to a $1 million fine and five years in prison [S3].
It permanently bars former members from paid lobbying and policy-influencing work, on penalty of up to $1 million and five years in prison [S3].
It requires the IRS to publish the last ten years of tax returns of anyone running for President or Vice President, with personal identifiers redacted [S3].

It bars the President, Vice President, Cabinet heads, and their immediate families from soliciting or raising money from foreign governments, foreign political parties, and entities they own or control [S3].
It extends the existing ban on foreign-national campaign contributions to state and local ballot initiatives and referenda [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Sitting members of Congress, who would have to give up individual stock trading, and former members, who would lose a lucrative path into lobbying; also firms that hire ex-lawmakers to influence government.
analysis.who_pays_short: Sitting and former members of Congress

drawbacks.text: The individual-stock ban still allows members to own and trade widely held investment funds, so members could retain diversified financial stakes in companies they regulate [S3].

The post-Congress lobbying ban is a lifetime prohibition with criminal penalties of up to five years in prison, far broader than the existing two-year cooling-off rule, which critics would say may unconstitutionally restrict former members' employment and push influence-seeking into less traceable channels [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's provisions were real and enforceable, backed by criminal penalties, and would have imposed modest costs on members (restricted investing, closed the lobbying door, forced tax disclosure) in exchange for a meaningful reduction in financial conflicts of interest in government. Main design critiques: allowing widely held funds means members can still hold broad market exposure to industries they regulate, and a lifetime lobbying ban (much broader than the existing two-year cooling-off rule) could push former members' influence into less transparent channels. On balance the costs were small and the transparency and anti-conflict gains were large; its death means none of those gains occurred.

outcome.mechanism: One senator introduced it, it went straight to the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: S. 3550 was introduced in the Senate on February 1, 2022 and read twice before being referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs [S1].
No senator signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The bill's action history ends with its referral to committee; it never received a markup, a floor vote, or any further action before the 117th Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Members of Congress and the lobbying industry are better off, since they avoided a stock-trading ban and a lifetime lobbying ban.

for.name: Sen. Ben Sasse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and saw it referred to committee; took no further recorded action on it.

against.name: Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no report — keeping it from the Senate floor.

against.name: The other 99 senators
against.what_they_did: None cosponsored the bill, leaving it without a coalition to press the committee for action.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Republican and drew no cosponsors from either party, so no partisan dividing line was ever tested.

industries.note: The bill would cut off the pipeline of former lawmakers selling their access to lobbying firms and corporate clients for life, removing a major talent source and revenue channel [S3].

industries.industry: Incumbent members of Congress and their families
industries.note: Members would lose the ability to trade individual stocks and former members the lucrative post-Congress lobbying market, eliminating personal financial opportunities created by their office [S3].
Members' trading would shift to diversified funds; the industry loses some high-profile individual-account business but keeps fund management for members [S3].
